paragraphs.heading: What snow is
paragraphs.text: Snow is solid precipitation made of separate ice crystals that grow while floating in the air, usually inside clouds, then fall and pile up on the ground. It stays frozen crystalline water through its whole life. The crystals form in the atmosphere, grow to about a millimetre, fall and settle, then change where they lie, and finally melt, slide off or sublimate away.

paragraphs.heading: How a crystal starts
paragraphs.text: A snow crystal starts when a tiny supercooled cloud droplet, about 10 μm across, freezes. Such droplets can stay liquid at temperatures below −18 °C, because freezing needs a few molecules to come together by chance into an ice-like pattern. That small cluster is the nucleus the droplet freezes around; in warmer clouds an aerosol particle, or ice nucleus, has to be present instead. A flake holds roughly 10¹⁹ water molecules, added at different rates as temperature and humidity change on the way down, so flakes differ while following similar patterns.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes of snowflakes
paragraphs.text: How crystals grow depends on many factors, including moisture and temperature. The results can be sorted into a few basic shapes and their combinations, chief among them platelets, needles, columns and rime. Now and then plate-like, branching or star-shaped flakes even form under a clear sky, when a very cold temperature inversion is present.

paragraphs.heading: Snow from storms and fronts
paragraphs.text: Snow clouds usually belong to larger weather systems, most importantly low-pressure areas with warm and cold fronts. Mid-latitude cyclones can produce anything from cloudiness and mild snow to heavy blizzards, and in the Northern Hemisphere the most snow falls on the northern side of the low. A cold front can bring a snowsquall, an intense line of convection that causes whiteouts with blowing snow; at any one spot it usually lasts under 30 minutes. A warm front can bring snow for a while as warm, moist air rides over freezing air, and the snow often turns to rain behind the front.

paragraphs.heading: Lake-effect snow
paragraphs.text: Lake-effect snow forms when a cold air mass crosses a long stretch of warmer lake water. The lowest air warms, takes up water vapour, rises through the colder air above, freezes and falls on the downwind shore. Over salt water the same thing is called ocean-effect or bay-effect snow. The bands can be narrow but very intense, dropping many inches an hour. The places hit are called snowbelts, such as the land east of the Great Lakes and the west coasts of northern Japan.

paragraphs.heading: Mountains, glaciers and shelter
paragraphs.text: In mountains, wind forces moist air up the windward slopes; the rising air cools, its moisture condenses and snow falls, leaving drier, warmer air on the far side. Where it stays cold enough for snow to build up year after year, a glacier may form. Elsewhere snow usually melts each season, feeding streams and rivers and refilling groundwater. In winter, snow cover also works as an insulating layer under which plants and animals survive the cold.
